claim: PLD2 is a mechanosensitive enzyme that is regulated by a structured membrane-lipid site comprised of cholesterol and saturated ganglioside (GM1).
source: Phospholipase D2 (PLD2) is a mechanosensitive enzyme that is regulated by a structured membrane-lipid site comprised of cholesterol and saturated ganglioside (GM1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript showing PLD2 interaction with GM1 and cholesterol.

claim: Stretch activation of TREK-1 is mechanically evoked by PLD2 and spatial patterning involving ordered GM1 and PIP2 clusters in mammalian cells.
source: Here we show stretch activation of TWIK-related K+ channel (TREK-1) is mechanically evoked by PLD2 and spatial patterning involving ordered GM1 and 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) clusters in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiology and imaging data in Figures 1-2.

claim: Mechanical force deforms ordered lipids, which disrupts the interaction of PLD2 with GM1 lipids.
source: First, mechanical force deforms the ordered lipids, which disrupts the interaction of PLD2 with the GM1 lipids and allows a complex of TREK-1 and PLD2 to associate with PIP2 clusters.
evidence: This mechanism is described in the abstract and supported by dSTORM imaging data in Figures 2-3 showing spatial reorganization.

claim: Association with PIP2 activates PLD2, which produces the second messenger phosphatidic acid (PA) that gates TREK-1.
source: The association with PIP2 activates the enzyme, which produces the second messenger phosphatidic acid (PA) that gates the channel.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by PLD activity assays and electrophysiology data showing PA-dependent channel gating.

claim: Co-expression of catalytically inactive PLD2 inhibits TREK-1 stretch currents in a biological membrane.
source: Co-expression of catalytically inactive PLD2 inhibits TREK-1 stretch currents in a biological membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by electrophysiology data in Figure 1B-C showing reduced currents with xPLD2.

claim: Cellular uptake of cholesterol inhibits TREK-1 currents in culture.
source: Cellular uptake of cholesterol inhibits TREK-1 currents in culture and depletion of cholesterol from astrocytes releases TREK-1 from GM1 lipids in mouse brain.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by whole-cell patch-clamp data in Figure 4D showing reduced current density with cholesterol loading.

claim: Depletion of cholesterol from astrocytes releases TREK-1 from GM1 lipids in mouse brain.
source: Cellular uptake of cholesterol inhibits TREK-1 currents in culture and depletion of cholesterol from astrocytes releases TREK-1 from GM1 lipids in mouse brain.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by dSTORM data from SREBP2 knockout mice in Figure 4E showing reduced TREK-1/GM1 correlation.

claim: Depletion of the PLD2 ortholog in flies results in hypersensitivity to mechanical force.
source: Depletion of the PLD2 ortholog in flies results in hypersensitivity to mechanical force.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by Drosophila behavioral data in Figure 6C-D showing decreased arousal thresholds.

claim: The overexpression of xPLD2 substantially inhibited nearly all mechanically evoked TREK-1 currents in intact HEK293T cells.
source: In intact HEK293T cells, the overexpression of xPLD2 substantially inhibited nearly all mechanically evoked TREK-1 currents (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by electrophysiology traces and quantification in Figure 1A-C.

claim: Mechanically evoked TREK-1 currents were reduced by over 80% when xPLD2 was overexpressed, from 0.181 ± 0.04 to 0.035 ± 0.013 pA/µm2.
source: When currents were measured in the inside out configuration under negative pressure conditions (from 0 to –60 mmHg), they exhibited a reduction of over 80% from 0.181 ± 0.04–0.035 ± 0.013 pA/µm2, despite an overall increase in the total levels of TREK-1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Specific quantitative measurements are provided with statistical data from electrophysiology experiments.

claim: Truncation of TREK-1 C-terminus at residue 322 decreased pressure-induced current by more than 85%, measuring 0.025 ± 0.013 pA/µm2.
source: The pressure-induced current in TREK trunc decreased by more than 85%, measuring 0.025 ± 0.013 pA/µm2 (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Quantitative data from electrophysiology experiments comparing truncated and full-length TREK-1.

claim: Previous studies have confirmed the functionality and mechanosensitivity of truncated TREK-1 when reconstituted into crude soy PC lipids.
source: Importantly, previous studies have confirmed the functionality and mechanosensitivity of this similar truncated TREK-1 when reconstituted into crude soy PC lipids (Brohawn et al., 2014a).
evidence: This claim references prior published work by Brohawn et al., 2014a.

claim: TREK-1 exhibited responsiveness to negative pressure with a half maximal pressure requirement of approximately 32 mmHg.
source: TREK-1 exhibited responsiveness to negative pressure (ranging from 0 to –60 mmHg, in a non-saturating regime) with a half maximal pressure requirement of approximately 32 mmHg.
evidence: Quantitative measurement of pressure sensitivity from electrophysiology experiments.

claim: TREK-1 is a mechanosensitive member of the two-pore-domain potassium (K2P) family known for its analgesic properties.
source: One of these channels is TWIK-related K+ channel subtype 1 (TREK-1), a mechanosensitive member of the two-pore-domain potassium (K2P) family known for its analgesic properties.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about TREK-1 properties.

claim: TREK-1 plays a role in inhibiting neuronal firing and reducing pain through the release of potassium ions.
source: TREK-1 plays a role in inhibiting neuronal firing and reducing pain through the release of potassium ions (Honoré, 2007).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Honoré, 2007.

claim: The enzyme phospholipase D2 (PLD2) directly interacts with the C-terminus of TREK-1, activating the channel by locally producing phosphatidic acid (PA).
source: Intriguingly, the enzyme phospholipase D2 (PLD2) directly interacts with the C-terminus of TREK-1, activating the channel by locally producing phosphatidic acid (PA) (Comoglio et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Comoglio et al., 2014.

claim: PLD2 exhibits mechanosensitivity despite lacking a transmembrane domain.
source: Despite lacking a transmembrane domain, PLD2 exhibits mechanosensitivity (Pavel et al., 2020; Petersen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Pavel et al., 2020 and Petersen et al., 2016.

claim: Palmitoylations of cysteine residues near PLD2's pleckstrin homology (PH) domain enable PLD2 to bind to a specific site composed of GM1 lipids and cholesterol in the liquid ordered region of the membrane.
source: Palmitoylations of cysteine residues near its pleckstrin homology (PH) domain enable PLD2 to bind to a specific site composed of monosialotetrahexosylganglioside (GM1) lipids and cholesterol in the liquid ordered (Lo) region of the membrane (McDermott et al., 2004; Yuan and Hansen, 2023; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated with citations and supported by a figure showing the mechanism.

claim: Application of mechanical force disrupts the AP site, releasing the palmitates of PLD2 and allowing the PH domain to interact with PIP2 clusters in the liquid disordered region of the membrane.
source: Application of mechanical force disrupts the AP site, releasing the palmitates of PLD2 and allowing the PH domain to interact with phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) clusters in the liquid disordered (Ld) region of the membrane (Petersen et al., 2016).
evidence: This mechanism is stated with a citation to Petersen et al., 2016.

claim: The C-terminus responsible for binding PLD2 is essential for TREK-1 mechanosensitivity in cellular membranes.
source: Notably, the C-terminus responsible for binding PLD2 is essential for TREK-1 mechanosensitivity in cellular membranes (Brohawn, 2015; Chemin et al., 2007a; Patel et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Brohawn, 2015; Chemin et al., 2007a; and Patel et al., 1998.

claim: Before the application of shear forces, TREK-1 and GM1 lipids displayed a robust correlation, suggesting a close association between TREK-1 and GM1 lipids.
source: Before the application of shear forces, TREK-1 and GM1 lipids displayed a robust correlation (Figure 2B and C), suggesting a close association between TREK-1 and GM1 lipids.
evidence: This is stated and supported by dSTORM imaging and pair correlation analysis in Figure 2B-C.

claim: After the application of shear forces, the correlation between TREK-1 and GM1 significantly diminished (p<0.01 at 50 nm).
source: However, after the application of shear forces, this correlation significantly diminished (p<0.01 at 50 nm).
evidence: Statistical analysis of dSTORM data showing decreased correlation after shear.

claim: The correlation between TREK-1 and PIP2 was initially low prior to shear application, but it significantly increased after shear forces were applied.
source: As predicted, the correlation between TREK-1 and PIP2 was initially low prior to shear application, but it significantly increased after shear forces were applied (Figure 2D), in contrast to the observations made with GM1 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated and supported by dSTORM imaging data in Figure 2D showing increased TREK-1/PIP2 correlation after shear.

claim: In the presence of xPLD2, shear caused TREK-1 to leave GM1 domains.
source: In the presence of xPLD2, shear caused TREK-1 to leave GM1 domains (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated and supported by dSTORM data in Figure 2E.

claim: Unlike the response observed with mPLD2, the association of TREK-1 with PIP2 clusters remained relatively weak following shear forces in the presence of xPLD2.
source: However, unlike the response observed with mPLD2, the association of TREK-1 with PIP2 clusters remained relatively weak following shear forces (Figure 2F), despite an overall increase in TREK-1 and PIP2 levels in the membrane prior to shear (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is stated and supported by dSTORM data comparing mPLD2 and xPLD2 conditions.

claim: Prior to the application of shear forces, PLD2 exhibited a strong association with GM1 clusters.
source: Prior to the application of shear forces, PLD2 exhibited a strong association with GM1 clusters (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated and supported by dSTORM pair correlation data in Figure 3B.

claim: After the application of shear forces, the correlation of PLD2 with GM1 clusters decreased significantly, while it robustly increased in association with PIP2 clusters.
source: However, after the application of shear forces, the correlation of PLD2 with GM1 clusters decreased significantly, while it robustly increased in association with PIP2 clusters (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated and supported by dSTORM data in Figure 3B-C showing PLD2 redistribution.

claim: Cluster analysis of GM1 particles subjected to shear revealed a notable reduction in the apparent size of GM1 clusters, decreasing from 167 ± 3 to 131 ± 3 nm (approximately 20%) in C2C12 cells.
source: Conducting cluster analysis of GM1 particles subjected to shear revealed a notable reduction in the apparent size of GM1 clusters, decreasing from 167 ± 3 to 131 ± 3 nm (approximately 20%, Figure 3D) in C2C12 cells.
evidence: Quantitative cluster analysis data from dSTORM imaging in Figure 3D.

claim: Results revealed a 25% reduction in free cholesterol levels in N2a cells exposed to orbital shear (p<0.001).
source: Our results revealed a 25% reduction in free cholesterol levels in N2a cells exposed to orbital shear (p<0.001) (Figure 3F), which coincided with the activation of PLD (Figure 3G).
evidence: Quantitative data from fluorescent cholesterol assay in Figure 3F.

claim: The decrease in cholesterol after shear was statistically significant (p<0.0001) and reversible.
source: Importantly, this decrease in cholesterol was statistically significant p<0.0001 and reversible.
evidence: Statistical analysis of cholesterol measurements showing significance and reversibility.

claim: Allowing the cells to recover for approximately 30 s prior to fixation resulted in the restoration of cholesterol levels to those observed in non-sheared cells.
source: Allowing the cells to recover for approximately 30 s prior to fixation resulted in the restoration of cholesterol levels to those observed in non-sheared cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: Experimental data showing reversibility of cholesterol changes in Figure 3F.

claim: Lipidated apoE induced a substantial clustering of TREK-1 with GM1 lipids in membranes of C2C12 cells.
source: Remarkably, lipidated apoE induced a substantial clustering of TREK-1 with GM1 lipids in membranes of C2C12 cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated and supported by dSTORM data in Figure 4B showing increased TREK-1/GM1 correlation with cholesterol.

claim: The application of fluid shear (3 dynes/cm2) completely reversed the effect of cholesterol on TREK-1 clustering with GM1.
source: Importantly, the application of fluid shear (3 dynes/cm2) completely reversed the effect of cholesterol (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated and supported by dSTORM data in Figure 4C.

claim: TREK-1 current density decreased nearly 2.5-fold in cholesterol-loaded cells, and this reduction in current was statistically significant (p<0.05).
source: Consistent with our proposed model, TREK-1 current density decreased nearly 2.5-fold in cholesterol-loaded cells, and this reduction in current was statistically significant (p<0.05).
evidence: Quantitative electrophysiology data from whole-cell patch-clamp experiments in Figure 4D.

claim: In flox control mice (wild-type SREBP2), TREK-1/GM1 correlation exhibited a distinct pattern, with TREK-1 clustering near GM1.
source: In flox control mice (wild-type SREBP2), TREK-1/GM1 correlation exhibited a distinct pattern, with TREK-1 clustering near GM1 (Figure 4E), aligning with the GM1 correlation seen in N2a cells with elevated levels of cholesterol (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated and supported by dSTORM data from brain slices in Figure 4E.

claim: In the brains of mice with astrocyte-specific SREBP2 deficiency, TREK-1 displayed a reduced association with GM1 lipids (p<0.0001).
source: As anticipated, in the brains of mice with astrocyte-specific SREBP2 deficiency, TREK-1 displayed a reduced association with GM1 lipids (p<0.0001).
evidence: Statistical analysis of dSTORM data from SREBP2 knockout mice showing reduced TREK-1/GM1 correlation.

claim: Membrane stretch by a 70 mOsm swell led to approximately 50% increase in PLD2 activity in N2a cells.
source: Our findings revealed that membrane stretch by a 70 mOsm swell (representing a high degree of stress) led to approximately 50% increase in PLD2 activity in N2a cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: Quantitative data from PLD activity assay in Figure 5A.

claim: dSTORM experiments demonstrated a discernible shift in the spatial distribution of PLD2, transitioning from ordered GM1 clusters to the PIP2 clusters after osmotic stretch.
source: Our results, consistent with the outcomes of shear stress experiments and PLD2 assay, clearly demonstrated a discernible shift in the spatial distribution of PLD2, transitioning from ordered GM1 clusters to the PIP2 clusters after osmotic stretch (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is stated and supported by dSTORM imaging data in Figure 5B-D.

claim: GM1 domains are present in dissected fly brains.
source: Our analysis revealed the presence of GM1 domains in dissected fly brains, and we observed that dPLD exhibited a robust response to shear stress of 3 dynes/cm2 when cultured in neuronally derived fly cell line, BG2-c2 (see Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is stated and supported by imaging data in Figure 6A showing CTxB labeling in fly brains.

claim: dPLD exhibited a robust response to shear stress of 3 dynes/cm2 when cultured in neuronally derived fly cell line, BG2-c2.
source: Our analysis revealed the presence of GM1 domains in dissected fly brains, and we observed that dPLD exhibited a robust response to shear stress of 3 dynes/cm2 when cultured in neuronally derived fly cell line, BG2-c2 (see Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is stated and supported by PLD activity assay data in Figure 6B.

claim: The activity of PLD increased by nearly fourfold in the fly cell line in response to shear.
source: The activity of PLD increased by nearly fourfold in the fly cell line (Figure 6B), a result consistent with the response of PLD to mechanical force observed in HEK293T cells (Figure 3G).
evidence: Quantitative data from PLD activity assay in fly cells in Figure 6B.

claim: PLDnull flies exhibited a notably lower arousal threshold compared to their control counterparts.
source: PLDnull flies exhibited a notably lower arousal threshold compared to their control counterparts (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated and supported by behavioral data in Figure 6C.

claim: The neuronal knockdown of PLD yielded a similar increase in mechanosensitivity, providing clear evidence that this phenotype is specific to neuronal functions.
source: Furthermore, we employed a neuronal-specific driver, Nsyb GAL4, in conjunction with a PLD RNAi line (PLD-KD) to investigate the role of PLD in the central nervous system. The neuronal knockdown of PLD yielded a similar increase in mechanosensitivity, providing clear evidence that this phenotype is specific to neuronal functions (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated and supported by behavioral data from PLD-KD flies in Figure 6D.

claim: PLDnull flies exhibited heightened sensitivity to electric shock compared to control groups.
source: Our findings revealed that PLDnull flies exhibited heightened sensitivity to electric shock compared to control groups (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is stated and supported by shock avoidance assay data in Figure 6E-F.

claim: The activation of purified TREK-1 in soy PC does not necessitate the involvement of the C-terminus.
source: In contrast, the activation of purified TREK-1 in soy PC does not necessitate the involvement of the C-terminus, as indicated by prior research (Brohawn et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Brohawn et al., 2014b.

claim: In HEK293T cells, a current density of 0.05 pA/cm2 current density (representing less than 10% of the total stretch current) was found to be PLD2 independent.
source: Notably, in HEK293T cells, a current density of 0.05 pA/cm2 current density (representing less than 10% of the total stretch current) was found to be PLD2 independent (see Figure 1C inset).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of electrophysiology data comparing different TREK-1 constructs.

claim: TREK-1 is directly activated by PA in purified lipids absent stretch and tension.
source: However, it is important to note that this enhancement mechanism is not obligatory as the channel is directly activated by PA in purified lipids absent stretch and tension (Cabanos et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Cabanos et al., 2017.

claim: Crude soy extracts (azolectin) are known to contain anionic lipids.
source: This can also explain the discrepancies between liposome-based mechanosensitivity since crude soy extracts (azolectin) are known to contain anionic lipids, thus may negate the need for a C-terminus and providing the PA needed for full TREK activation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about soy lipid composition.

claim: The palmate moiety establishes van der Waals bonds with the GM1 lipids.
source: The palmate moiety establishes van der Waals bonds with the GM1 lipids.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on molecular interactions.

claim: The disruption of van der Waals bonds is necessary for PLD to disassociate from GM1 lipids, suggesting a mechanism akin to 'shear thinning' within GM1 clusters.
source: The disruption of these bonds is necessary for PLD to disassociate from GM1 lipids, suggesting a mechanism akin to 'shear thinning' within GM1 clusters.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: Initial TREK-1 currents were observed almost immediately and became notably significant within 2.1 ms at a pressure of 60 mmHg.
source: We observed initial TREK-1 currents almost immediately and these currents became notably significant within 2.1 ms at a pressure of 60 mmHg (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Temporal analysis of electrophysiology data showing rapid activation kinetics.

claim: TREK-1 is a potassium leak channel with inherent basal currents in cultured cells.
source: TREK-1 is a potassium leak channel with inherent basal currents in cultured cells (Comoglio et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Comoglio et al., 2014.

claim: TREK-1 basal current was observed both in the presence (16.9 ± 4.3 pA/pF) and absence (24.0 ± 4.2 pA/pF) of xPLD2.
source: As anticipated, we observed TREK-1 basal current both in the presence (16.9 ± 4.3 pA/pF) and absence (24.0 ± 4.2 pA/pF) of xPLD2 (Comoglio et al., 2014; Figure 1D).
evidence: Quantitative electrophysiology data from whole-cell recordings in Figure 1D.

claim: Palmitoylation is a modification found in many important signaling molecules including tyrosine kinases, GTPases, CD4/8, and almost all G-protein alpha subunits.
source: Palmitoylation, a modification found in many important signaling molecules including tyrosine kinases, GTPases, CD4/8, and almost all G-protein alpha subunits (Aicart-Ramos et al., 2011), can target proteins to GM1 domains (Levental et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Aicart-Ramos et al., 2011 and Levental et al., 2010.

claim: Palmitoylation can target proteins to GM1 domains.
source: Palmitoylation, a modification found in many important signaling molecules including tyrosine kinases, GTPases, CD4/8, and almost all G-protein alpha subunits (Aicart-Ramos et al., 2011), can target proteins to GM1 domains (Levental et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Levental et al., 2010.

claim: The voltage-gated sodium channel (Nav)1.9 clusters with GM1 lipids, and disrupting this clustering induces a corresponding pain response.
source: For example, the voltage-gated sodium channel (Nav)1.9 clusters with GM1 lipids, and disrupting this clustering (e.g., by chemically removing cholesterol) induces a corresponding pain response (Amsalem et al., 2018; Wan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Amsalem et al., 2018 and Wan et al., 2018.

claim: S1P, an anionic lipid similar to PA, regulates pain in mice.
source: Similarly, S1P, an anionic lipid similar to PA, regulates pain in mice (Hill et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Hill et al., 2018.

claim: PIP2 gates many ion channels.
source: It is worth noting that PIP2 gates many ion channels (Cabanos et al., 2017; Chung et al., 2019; Hansen, 2015; Hansen et al., 2011; Robinson et al., 2019), and the spatial patterning induced by PIP2 should be considered in combination with the direct effect of the lipid on the channel.
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: Cholesterol is known to bind directly to and modulate channels.
source: Cholesterol, known to bind directly to and modulate channels (Levitan et al., 2014), should also be considered separately from its influence on spatial patterning through GM1 lipids.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Levitan et al., 2014.

claim: Combined paraformaldehyde and glutaraldehyde effectively inhibited GM1 lipid diffusion, as confirmed by FRAP experiments.
source: In our system, combined paraformaldehyde and glutaraldehyde effectively inhibited GM1 lipid diffusion, as confirmed by fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) experiments conducted in live cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: This is stated and supported by FRAP data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: HEK293T cells were selected for this study due to their minimal endogenous potassium currents.
source: We selected HEK293T cells for this study due to their minimal endogenous potassium currents, which allowed us to attribute the recorded currents specifically to TREK-1.
evidence: This is a methodological justification stated in the Results section.

claim: The expression of TREK-1 was tracked using an EGFP tag attached to the channel's C-terminus.
source: The expression of TREK-1 was tracked using an EGFP tag attached to the channels C-terminus, and we confirmed successful expression of all constructs, observing their presence on the cell surface (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by imaging data.

claim: xPLD2 expression is >10× the endogenous PLD2 (enPLD2).
source: The xPLD2 expression is >10× the endogenous PLD2 (enPLD2) that we previously showed outcompetes the binding of enPLD2 to TREK-1 under similar conditions (Pavel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Pavel et al., 2020.

claim: TREK-1 exhibited responsiveness to negative pressure with a half maximal pressure requirement of approximately 32 mmHg, which led to the generation of up to 200 pA of TREK-1 current.
source: TREK-1 exhibited responsiveness to negative pressure (ranging from 0 to –60 mmHg, in a non-saturating regime) with a half maximal pressure requirement of approximately 32 mmHg. This pressure led to the generation of up to 200 pA of TREK-1 current (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), aligning with findings from prior investigations (Brohawn et al., 2014b; Patel et al., 1998).
evidence: Quantitative electrophysiology data with citations to prior work.

claim: TREK trunc exhibited a modest increase in current, measuring 0.046 ± 0.023 pA/µm2 (p=0.08), when compared to the condition with no TREK-1.
source: Our results demonstrated that TREK trunc exhibited a modest increase in current, measuring 0.046 ± 0.023 pA/µm2 (p=0.08, Figure 1C inset), when compared to the condition with no TREK-1.
evidence: Quantitative electrophysiology data comparing truncated TREK-1 to mock transfection.

claim: In cells expressing xPLD2 alongside full-length TREK-1, the channel exhibited a small increase in current measuring 0.060 ± 0.035 pA/µm2 (p=0.11).
source: Similarly, in cells expressing xPLD2 alongside full-length TREK-1, the channel exhibited a small increase in current measuring 0.060 ± 0.035 pA/µm2 (p=0.11).
evidence: Quantitative electrophysiology data from cells with xPLD2.

claim: PIP2 forms distinct nanodomains that are separate from GM1 clusters by an average distance of approximately 133 nm in HEK293T cells.
source: PIP2 forms distinct nanodomains that are separate from GM1 clusters (Petersen et al., 2016; van den Bogaart et al., 2011; Wang and Richards, 2012) by an average distance of approximately 133 nm in HEK293T cells (Yuan et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations including Yuan et al., 2022.

claim: Astrocytes play a pivotal role in regulating the clustering of proteins in neurons through the release of apoE-containing particles laden with cholesterol.
source: In our earlier investigation, we established that astrocytes play a pivotal role in regulating the clustering of proteins in neurons. This regulation is achieved through the release of apoE-containing particles, which are primarily laden with cholesterol.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work by the authors.

claim: Cholesterol amplifies the clustering of proteins within GM1 domains.
source: Remarkably, our studies revealed that cholesterol amplifies the clustering of proteins within GM1 domains.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work by the authors.

claim: Disrupting the cholesterol synthesis in astrocytes leads to the reversal of protein clustering.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that disrupting the cholesterol synthesis in astrocytes leads to the reversal of protein clustering, as previously reported (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Wang et al., 2021.

claim: The depletion of cholesterol from astrocytes was achieved by targeting sterol regulatory element-binding protein 2 (SREBP2), a crucial regulator of cholesterol synthesis.
source: The depletion of cholesterol from astrocytes was achieved by targeting sterol regulatory element-binding protein 2 (SREBP2), a crucial regulator of cholesterol synthesis (Ferris et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a methodological description with citations.

claim: Flies lack a known mechanosensitive TREK-1 homolog.
source: It is worth noting that, while the specific downstream effectors of PLD in fruit flies remain unidentified, and they possess only distantly related TREK-1 orthologs, (as discussed in a later section), the utilization of fruit flies as a model organism is advantageous because they possess a single PLD gene (dPLD).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about Drosophila genetics.

claim: Fruit flies possess a single PLD gene (dPLD).
source: It is worth noting that, while the specific downstream effectors of PLD in fruit flies remain unidentified, and they possess only distantly related TREK-1 orthologs, (as discussed in a later section), the utilization of fruit flies as a model organism is advantageous because they possess a single PLD gene (dPLD).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about Drosophila genetics.

claim: PIP2 sets the threshold for mechanical B-cell activation.
source: For example, PIP2 sets the threshold for mechanical B-cell activation (Wan et al., 2018), while sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P), a lipid similar to PA, regulates pain in mice (Hill et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Wan et al., 2018.

claim: The activation of PLD2 by mechanical force and substrate presentation helps elucidate how an enzyme could directly set pain thresholds and mechanosensitivity via canonical mechanosensitive ion channels and endocytosis.
source: The activation of PLD2 by mechanical force and substrate presentation helps elucidate how an enzyme could directly set pain thresholds and mechanosensitivity via canonical mechanosensitive ion channels and endocytosis.
evidence: This is a concluding interpretation of the findings in the Discussion.

claim: Many ion channels are palmitoylated.
source: Many ion channels are also palmitoylated (Shipston, 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Shipston, 2011.

claim: Antibody patching has historically served as a useful tool to segregate proteins within biological membrane, facilitating the determination of their precise localization.
source: Antibody patching has historically served as a useful tool to segregate proteins within biological membrane, facilitating the determination of their precise localization (Lang et al., 2001; Yuan and Hansen, 2023).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Lang et al., 2001 and Yuan and Hansen, 2023.

claim: The pair correlation function is a method that is robust against artifacts associated with changes in labeling density.
source: The mechanical disruption of PLD2 with GM1 lipids and its association with PIP2 was determined by the pair correlation function, a method that is robust against artifacts associated with changes in labeling density (Coltharp et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Coltharp et al., 2014.

claim: xPLD2 has been shown to inhibit both agonist-induced and constitutive endocytosis of µ-opioid receptor, effectively retaining the receptor on the membrane.
source: Specifically, xPLD2 has been shown to inhibit both agonist-induced and constitutive endocytosis of µ-opioid receptor, effectively retaining the receptor on the membrane (Koch et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Koch et al., 2006.

claim: The overexpression of mPLD led to the lowest levels of TREK-1 expression, which aligns with its propensity for promoting endocytosis.
source: Conversely, the overexpression of mPLD led to the lowest levels of TREK_1 expression, which aligns with its propensity for promoting endocytosis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: This is stated and supported by imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: The latency for PLD2-dependent activation was estimated at ~650 μs based on diffusion from GM1 to PIP2.
source: Drawing from estimates involving diffusion from GM1 to PIP2, we estimated a latency of ~650 μs (Petersen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an estimate based on prior work cited as Petersen et al., 2016.

claim: TREK-1 currents became notably significant within 2.1 ms at a pressure of 60 mmHg, which is highly likely to be faster than the margin of error associated with the instrument setup.
source: We observed initial TREK-1 currents almost immediately and these currents became notably significant within 2.1 ms at a pressure of 60 mmHg (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D). This time frame is highly likely to be faster than the margin of error associated with our instrument setup.
evidence: This is stated based on temporal analysis of electrophysiology data.

claim: Conservative estimates based on manufacturer specifications suggest an upper limit of approximately 10 ms for the instrument setup error.
source: While we did not perform a precise calibration of our setup's error, conservative estimates based on manufacturer specifications suggest an upper limit of approximately 10 ms.
evidence: This is an estimate based on instrument specifications.
